scenes.heading: Pedigree charts
scenes.say: We can't breed humans in controlled crosses. So how do geneticists work out how a trait is inherited? They trace it through a family, using a pedigree chart.

scenes.heading: Reading the symbols
points: Generations: I, II, III from the top
II-3 = 3rd person from left in generation II
scenes.say: Squares are males and circles are females. A shaded shape means affected. Generations are labelled with Roman numerals from the top, and people are numbered from left to right. So two dash three is the third person in generation two.
scenes.caption: Squares are males and circles are females. A shaded shape means affected. Generations are labelled with Roman numerals from the top, and people are numbered from left to right. So II-3 is the third person in generation II.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A detective crosses suspects off using alibis
scenes.science: Rule out modes of inheritance using key clues
scenes.breaks: A detective usually finds one culprit. A small pedigree may leave more than one mode possible.
scenes.say: Reading a pedigree is like being a detective. The four modes of inheritance are your suspects: autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive and X-linked dominant. Each clue is an alibi that crosses a suspect off. Whoever's left is your answer. But sometimes, more than one stays possible.

scenes.heading: The two clinchers
scenes.say: Start with the two clinchers. If two unaffected parents have an affected child, the trait is recessive. If two affected parents have an unaffected child, it's dominant.

scenes.heading: Ruling out X-linked
points: XR: affected female needs affected father
XR: all her sons are affected
XD: affected male → ALL daughters affected
XD: and none of his sons
scenes.say: For X-linked recessive, an affected female must have an affected father, and all her sons will be affected. If not, rule it out. For X-linked dominant, an affected father passes the trait to all his daughters and none of his sons.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Unaffected parents I-1 and I-2 have an affected daughter, II-2, and two unaffected children. What is the mode of inheritance?
lines: So X-linked recessive is ruled out
scenes.say: Unaffected parents, one dash one and one dash two, have an affected daughter. Unaffected parents with an affected child means recessive. Could it be X-linked recessive? No: an affected female would need an affected father, and hers isn't. So it's autosomal recessive.
scenes.caption: Unaffected parents, I-1 and I-2, have an affected daughter. Unaffected parents with an affected child means recessive. Could it be X-linked recessive? No: an affected female would need an affected father, and hers isn't. So it's autosomal recessive.

scenes.heading: Two-thirds, not a half
steps: Aa × Aa → AA, Aa, Aa, aa
Child is unaffected: rule out aa
scenes.say: What's the chance an unaffected child of two carriers is a carrier? The Punnett square gives four outcomes. But the child is unaffected, so cross off the affected one. Of the three left, two are carriers. So the chance is two thirds, not a half.

points: Use XR and XD rules to rule out
scenes.say: Quick recap. Unaffected parents with an affected child means recessive. Affected parents with an unaffected child means dominant. Use the X-linked rules to rule patterns out, and quote specific people. And remember: two thirds, not a half. Now try the practice questions!
